question.context: Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis (XGC) is an uncommon variant of chronic cholecystitis, characterized by marked thickening of the gallbladder wall and dense local adhesions. It often mimics a gallbladder carcinoma (GBC), and may coexist with GBC, leading to a diagnostic dilemma. Furthermore, the premalignant nature of this entity is not known. This study was undertaken to assess the p53, PCNA and beta-catenin expression in XGC in comparison to GBC and chronic inflammation. Sections from paraffin-embedded blocks of surgically resected specimens of GBC (69 cases), XGC (65), chronic cholecystitis (18) and control gallbladder (10) were stained with the monoclonal antibodies to p53 and PCNA, and a polyclonal antibody to beta-catenin. p53 expression was scored as the percentage of nuclei stained. PCNA expression was scored as the product of the percentage of nuclei stained and the intensity of the staining (1-3). A cut-off value of 80 for this score was taken as a positive result. Beta-catenin expression was scored as type of expression-membranous, cytoplasmic or nuclear staining. p53 mutation was positive in 52% of GBC cases and 3% of XGC, but was not expressed in chronic cholecystitis and control gallbladders. p53 expression was lower in XGC than in GBC (P<0.0001). PCNA expression was seen in 65% of GBC cases and 11% of XGC, but not in chronic cholecystitis and control gallbladders. PCNA expression was higher in GBC than XGC (P=0.0001), but there was no significant difference between the XGC, chronic cholecystitis and control gallbladder groups. Beta-catenin expression was positive in the GBC, XGC, chronic cholecystitis and control gallbladder groups. But the expression pattern in XGC, chronic cholecystitis and control gallbladders was homogenously membranous, whereas in GBC the membranous expression pattern was altered to cytoplasmic and nuclear.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found a significantly higher p53 mutation rate in GBC (52%) compared to XGC (3%). This suggests a higher likelihood of malignancy in GBC. While XGC can mimic GBC, the p53 mutation data leans towards a premalignant nature.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: p53 mutation was positive in 52% of GBC cases and 3% of XGC.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: The study also considered chronic cholecystitis and control gallbladders. The absence of p53 mutations in these groups further supports the idea that XGC is a premalignant condition, as it is more likely to be associated with malignancy than chronic inflammation or normal gallbladder tissue.

rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: p53 expression is significantly lower in XGC (3%) compared to GBC (52%), indicating absence of tumor suppressor mutation seen in cancer.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Gallbladder carcinoma (GBC) was considered but ruled out by molecular markers; chronic cholecystitis was considered but XGC shows more severe wall thickening and adhesions

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study shows that XGC has significantly lower p53 and PCNA expression compared to GBC, which are markers of malignancy and cellular proliferation. The absence of p53 mutations and low proliferative activity in XGC suggests it is not premalignant. Additionally, beta-catenin expression patterns in XGC are similar to benign conditions, further supporting its non-malignant nature.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: p53 mutation was positive in 52% of GBC cases but only 3% of XGC cases, with significantly lower p53 expression in XGC (P<0.0001), indicating a lack of malignant transformation.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Gallbladder carcinoma was considered due to the morphological mimicry, but ruled out by molecular markers showing low proliferative and mutational activity in XGC compared to GBC.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: GBC is the obvious malignancy with high p53 and PCNA expression and nuclear/cytoplasmic alterations in beta-catenin. Chronic cholecystitis and normal gallbladder show no such markers, further differentiating them from malignancy. However, XGC may have a spectrum of dysplasia, so it is not definitively ruled out as premalignant.
